solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique, directions as headed); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Bet on passion in rebound

blocks.note: to back a horse is to bet on it
fire is ardour or passion

explanation.surface: A gambler's passionate wager is placed while their fortunes are on the rebound.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bet on' reads as one phrase in the surface but supplies the first half; 'in' simply joins wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A plan that recoils on its maker is said to backfire, the same idea as a scheme that rebounds.

clue.text: Stain Antony twice discovered under the table

indicators.note: to discover is to take the cover off, and doing it two times strips two layers from each end

blocks.note: a blot is a stain or smudge
the name loses its outer letters twice over, leaving the central pair

explanation.surface: Someone notices a stain on Antony's clothes, perhaps from a dinner party that went too far.
explanation.walkthrough: Removing the outside letters once leaves NTON; doing it again leaves TO. 'Under the table' is the idiom for very drunk.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone drunk enough to slide off their chair is under the table, and blotto is slang for heavily intoxicated.

clue.text: Trees, possibly sacred …

indicators.note: what is only possible is one arrangement among several, so the letters may be reordered

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis runs on into the next clue, which uses these trees as its subject; here the clue stands alone as a definition plus rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: The cedar is a tall coniferous evergreen, famously the cedar of Lebanon, so the plural names several such conifers.

clue.text: … could be used for this English forest following another tree

definitions.note: a clause pointing back to the previous answer, meaning 'what cedars could become'

indicators.note: to follow is to come after, so what is named before this word goes at the back

blocks.note: a fir is a tree other than the cedars of the previous clue
E is the standard abbreviation for English
a wood is a small forest

explanation.surface: Continuing from the cedars: trees from an English forest could end up being used for something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Following' tells you the tree comes first and the English forest after it. The definition only makes sense read with the previous clue: cedars could be used for this.
explanation.definitionFit: Felled cedar logs are burnt as fuel, so cut timber destined for the grate is what cedars could serve as.

clue.text: Mechanical repetition featured in rhetorician’s retreat

indicators.note: something featured in a thing appears inside it, so the letters sit within the words that follow
to retreat is to go backwards, so the letters are read the other way

blocks.note: the second to fifth letters of the word

explanation.surface: A public speaker withdraws into the habit of repeating the same lines mechanically.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Retreat' looks like a noun, a rhetorician's hideaway, but it is a verb telling you to read the hidden letters backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Learning by rote means memorising through mechanical repetition rather than real understanding, as children chant tables.

clue.text: Male after one-fifth off fast food

indicators.note: taking off a fifth of a five-letter word means dropping a single letter
placing one item after another sets them side by side in that sequence

blocks.note: quick means fast; its last letter is dropped
he is the male pronoun

explanation.surface: A man finds that his fast food has had a fifth knocked off its price.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fast food' reads as a single phrase, but 'fast' belongs to the wordplay and 'food' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A quiche is a savoury egg-and-pastry tart, an example of something to eat.

clue.text: Hunt, at heart absolutely not fair

indicators.note: the heart of something is its centre, so only the central letters are kept

blocks.note: the two central letters of the word
just can mean absolutely, as in 'just perfect'

explanation.surface: Someone protests that a hunt is, deep down, thoroughly unfair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hunt' with a capital looks like a person's name, but it is just the word supplying its centre.
explanation.definitionFit: An unjust decision violates fairness and equity; the prefix negates just, which itself means fair.

clue.text: Breakdown service returns cards and takes over vehicle

indicators.note: to return is to come back, so the letters run the opposite way

blocks.note: the RAC (Royal Automobile Club) is a British roadside breakdown organisation
jacks are playing cards

explanation.surface: A motoring rescue service hands back some cards and then commandeers a car.
explanation.walkthrough: The RAC is one of Britain's two big roadside rescue clubs, alongside the AA; 'returns' turns its letters around.
explanation.definitionFit: To carjack is to seize a motor by force from its driver, so the verb with an s means hijacks an automobile.

clue.text: Facility is seen as strange

indicators.note: something strange is odd or out of order, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A building or amenity is regarded as odd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Facility' suggests a building, but here it means ease or skill, as in doing something with great facility.
explanation.definitionFit: Facility can mean a natural ability to do something without effort, which is lack of difficulty.

clue.text: Throw out bread that’s hard

indicators.note: to throw something is to toss it about, so the letters land in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Stale bread that has gone hard should be thrown out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Throw out' reads as a phrasal verb, but 'out' is part of the letters to be rearranged and 'Throw' alone is the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Obdurate means stubbornly unyielding or hard-hearted, refusing to be moved by persuasion.

clue.text: Beginning of jarring in car manufacturer’s inlets

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its opening letter, so only that is taken
a thing placed in another sits inside it, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: the first letter of the word
Ford is a car maker; with the possessive it reads as FORD'S

explanation.surface: A jolt begins as a car maker's vehicle drives through some coastal inlets.
explanation.walkthrough: The possessive on the car maker supplies the final S, slotted round the single letter after F.
explanation.definitionFit: Fjords are long, narrow sea inlets between steep cliffs, typical of Norway's coastline.

clue.text: Rural peer, randy on vacation

indicators.note: to vacate is to empty out, so only the outside letters remain

blocks.note: a count is a nobleman, a peer
the first and last letters of the word

explanation.surface: A lustful nobleman from the shires goes off on holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On vacation' sounds like a holiday but signals emptying the word it follows. Randy is British slang for lustful.
explanation.definitionFit: Country used as an adjective, as in country life, means relating to the countryside rather than towns.

clue.text: Baffled cast

blocks.note: first meaning: confused, disconcerted
second meaning: hurled or tossed, the past participle

explanation.walkthrough: Two words side by side read like a description of puzzled actors, but each is a separate meaning of the same past participle.
explanation.definitionFit: Being thrown by a question means being disconcerted, while a ball that has been cast has been hurled.

clue.text: One leading the way announced bird’s decline

indicators.note: an announcement is spoken out, so the answer is what the words sound like

blocks.note: cocks are male birds and to wane is to decline

explanation.surface: Someone at the front of a group reports that a bird population is falling.
explanation.walkthrough: The sound match relies on the spelling pronunciation; rowers usually say 'coxun'. The cox steers the boat, so leads the crew's way.
explanation.definitionFit: A coxswain steers a rowing boat and directs the crew, guiding the vessel along its course.

clue.text: Look to cover English races in paper

indicators.note: covering something means wrapping round it, so one piece surrounds the rest

blocks.note: to gaze is to look steadily
E is the standard abbreviation for English
the TT (Tourist Trophy) races are motorcycle races on the Isle of Man

explanation.surface: Someone checks the newspaper for its coverage of horse races in England.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cover' suggests press reporting, but here the gazing word wraps around English plus races.
explanation.definitionFit: Gazette is a traditional name for a newspaper, especially an official journal of record.

clue.text: Eggs containing key salad ingredient

indicators.note: containing means holding inside, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: roe is fish eggs
main as an adjective means chief or key

explanation.surface: Eggs form a key part of a salad.
explanation.walkthrough: The eggs are fish eggs, a common crossword source for these three letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Romaine is cos lettuce, a long-leaved variety used in Caesar salad.

clue.text: Runners smooch when son moves into the lead

indicators.note: S is the abbreviation for son, and moving it from behind to the front rotates the closing letter round to the start

blocks.note: to smooch is to kiss

explanation.surface: Two racers are caught kissing as one's son overtakes them to take the lead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Runners' suggests athletes, but skis are runners in the sense of the blades a sledge glides on.
explanation.definitionFit: Runners are the long narrow strips on which sledges and snow vehicles slide, and skis are such strips.

clue.text: Film buff is at a broadcast

indicators.note: to broadcast originally meant to scatter seed widely, so the letters are scattered

blocks.note: a buff is an enthusiast or fan
taken as written

explanation.surface: A cinema enthusiast attends a screening that is being broadcast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Film buff' reads as one phrase, but 'Film' alone is the definition and 'buff' starts the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Fantasia is the 1940 Disney animated feature set to classical music, a famous motion picture.

clue.text: Paying a call is involved in proposing a meeting not at home

indicators.note: 'not' says the following item is absent, so those letters are removed
to be involved in something is to be caught up inside it, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: inviting someone is proposing they meet you
being in means being at home
taken as written

explanation.surface: Paying a social call involves suggesting a get-together when nobody is at home.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove 'at home' from the inviting word to get VITING, then insert IS after the V.
explanation.definitionFit: Visiting someone means calling on them at their home, the same as making a social call.

clue.text: Bill right to seek answer: where does Lincoln makes the laws?

definitions.text: where does Lincoln makes the laws?

blocks.note: neb is an old word for a bird's beak or bill
R is the standard abbreviation for right
to ask for something is to seek it
A is the standard abbreviation for answer

explanation.surface: A lawmaker seeks an answer about where Abraham Lincoln once passed laws.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bill' and 'laws' suggest legislation, but the bill is a bird's beak. Lincoln here is not the president but the city.
explanation.definitionFit: Lincoln is the state capital of Nebraska, home of its legislature, so this US state is where Lincoln passes laws.

clue.text: A cricket team succeeded in alliance

blocks.note: taken as written
a cricket side has eleven players, written XI in Roman numerals
S is the abbreviation for succeeded, used in family trees

explanation.surface: A cricket side has done well thanks to working in partnership.
explanation.walkthrough: A cricket team is eleven players, hence the Roman numeral XI.
explanation.definitionFit: An axis is a pact between powers, most famously the Axis of Germany, Italy and Japan in the Second World War.

clue.text: Group of students getting new education sighed

blocks.note: a year is a school cohort, as in Year 9
N is the standard abbreviation for new
ED is the abbreviation for education

explanation.surface: A class of pupils sighed on being told about a new educational scheme.
explanation.walkthrough: In British schools pupils are grouped by year, so a year is a group of students.
explanation.definitionFit: To sigh for something is to long for it, so sighed in that sense means longed or pined.

clue.text: Archdeacon always in disguise

blocks.note: an archdeacon is styled the Venerable, abbreviated Ven
e'er is the poetic contraction of ever, meaning always

explanation.surface: A senior clergyman is forever going about in disguise.
explanation.walkthrough: In the Church of England an archdeacon carries the title 'the Venerable', shortened to Ven.
explanation.definitionFit: A veneer is a thin attractive surface layer hiding what lies beneath, so figuratively a false front.

clue.text: Great heat and light rain making month squally at first

indicators.note: what comes at first is the opening, so only the initial letter is used
making one thing into another changes it, so a letter is swapped for a different one

blocks.note: mizzle is a dialect word for fine drizzle
M is the abbreviation for month; this is the letter replaced
the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A month that begins with squalls brings both scorching heat and light rain.
explanation.walkthrough: Mizzle, a mix of mist and drizzle, has its M changed to S.
explanation.definitionFit: Sizzle is used for intense, scorching hot weather, from the hissing of food frying in a hot pan.

clue.text: It’s mad, mad, in ‘The Thick of It’

definitions.note: the definition is 'in the thick of', with the title's final word carried along

indicators.note: something mad is crazy and disordered, so the letters are thrown into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written; the first copy of the repeated word is part of the letters

explanation.surface: A viewer exclaims that everything is utterly crazy in the British political satire The Thick of It.
explanation.walkthrough: The repeated word does two jobs: the first is letters, the second the signal. The Thick of It is a BBC comedy about chaotic government.
explanation.definitionFit: Amidst means surrounded by or in the middle of, exactly what being in the thick of something means.

clue.text: Shelters including free weapons

indicators.note: including something means taking it in, so one piece is held inside the other

blocks.note: tents are temporary shelters
to rid is to free, as in rid of pests

explanation.surface: Refuges that stock arms for anyone who wants them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Free' looks like an adjective about the weapons, but it is the verb meaning to clear.
explanation.definitionFit: A trident is a three-pronged spear, used as a weapon by Roman gladiators and carried by Neptune.

clue.text: ‘Honestly, no energy’ is start of matrimonial platitude

indicators.note: 'no' says something is absent, so that letter is taken out
the start of a word is its first letter, so only that is kept

blocks.note: true as an adverb means honestly, as in 'speak true'; it loses its E
E is the symbol for energy; this is the letter removed
taken as written
the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A spouse's tired excuse about lacking energy is the opening line of a marital cliché.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Honestly' gives TRUE, used adverbially; dropping E leaves TRU.
explanation.definitionFit: A truism is a statement so obviously correct that it is trite, which is what a platitude is.

clue.text: Leave quietly, no time for pleasantry

indicators.note: 'no' says the item named next is absent, so that letter is taken out

blocks.note: to quit is to leave
p (piano) is the musical marking for quietly
T is the abbreviation for time; this is the letter removed

explanation.surface: Someone slips away silently, with no time for small talk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leave quietly' reads as one instruction but is two pieces; P is the musical marking piano.
explanation.definitionFit: A pleasantry can be a light joking remark, and a quip is a witty one-liner of that kind.

clue.text: Turn left following cycling partners

indicators.note: cycling means going round in a loop, so the letters rotate with the end coming to the front
one item following another comes after it, setting the pieces in order

blocks.note: wives are marriage partners
L is the standard abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: A cyclist is told to turn left after their riding companions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cycling partners' looks like cyclists, but 'cycling' tells you to move the last letter of the wives to the front.
explanation.definitionFit: To swivel is to rotate around a fixed point, so it means turn, as a chair does.

clue.text: Enormous omissions in short final letter

indicators.note: something cut short has been trimmed before reaching its natural end, losing its tail

blocks.note: outs are things left out, especially in printing
the word minus its final letter
zed is the British name for the last letter of the alphabet

explanation.surface: Huge gaps appear in a brief last letter someone has written.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like a container signal but is itself shortened. 'Final letter' means the end of the alphabet, not a last piece of correspondence.
explanation.definitionFit: Outsized describes something larger than the usual size, so very big or huge.

clue.text: A surge up occasionally tracks forecast

indicators.note: occasionally means every so often, so only every other letter is kept

blocks.note: the odd-numbered letters of these words
RY is the abbreviation for railway, which runs on tracks

explanation.surface: A forecaster predicts a periodic upward surge along railway lines.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Up' looks like a direction signal, but it is just part of the letters being thinned out.
explanation.definitionFit: An augury is an omen or prophecy, originally the Roman practice of foretelling events from birds.

clue.text: Father sent back by himself? That’s obvious

indicators.note: something sent back goes in the opposite direction, so its letters are read backwards

blocks.note: pa is an informal word for father
himself refers back to the father, who is a parent

explanation.surface: A father is returned home by himself, and it is plain to see why.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Himself' points back at the father, so the second piece is another word for him.
explanation.definitionFit: Apparent means clearly visible or understood, plain to see, the same as evident.
